While the poster admits the BTC figure looks absurd compared with the rest, he is mostly gutted that his license exam is still pending. The thread quickly turned into a collective lament over missed generational wealth, with anons weighing in on whether piling into BTC at this stage is already late or whether…
clips.text_en_c1: A /biz/ infographic illustrates the cumulative returns one would have realised by allocating a mere $1,000 fifteen years prior: Bitcoin has appreciated to roughly $8.97 million, Nvidia to $735,000, Tesla to $231,000, Apple to $29,000, the S&P 500 to $8,400, and gold to $2,150. The original poster, visibly despondent, fixates on the BTC figure, remarking that its sheer magnitude renders every alternative asset laughable by comparison. He laments having yet to secure his professional licence, observing that ordinary people were priced out of generational wealth by inaction. Underneath, anons cite missed opportunities, lamenting that foresight, however imperfect, would have sufficed, given how the asset class has compounded.
clips.text_en_c2: A chart disseminated across /biz/ lays out the cumulative returns one would have accrued by investing a modest $1,000 fifteen years prior: Bitcoin towers above the field at $8,970,000, Nvidia trails at a still-stratospheric $735,000, Tesla claims $231,000, Apple limps to $29,000, the S&P 500 inches up to $8,400, while gold, the supposed store of value, yields a measly $2,150. The poster, evidently a Hong Kong resident still pursuing a professional licence, finds the disparity almost unbearable to contemplate, observing that Bitcoin's number is so patently absurd against every other comparator that the entire exercise feels like a cruel joke.

clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI formally unveiled GPT-6 Astra on Thursday, accompanied by the now-customary flourish in which the company declared the model the most intelligent and most rigorously aligned system yet constructed, and accordingly welcomed all observers to what it grandly termed the AGI era. clips.text_en_b1: A /pol/ poster flew into Helsinki airport and saw nothing but foreigners. Then he took the train to Tampere, Oulu, and Rovaniemi, and it was the same story. He is shocked that even small northern Finnish cities are full of Indians and other immigrants now.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread complaining about immigration across Finland
clips.text_en_b2: A /pol/ poster landed at Helsinki airport and noticed nothing but foreigners, only to find that the same picture held on the train up to Tampere, Oulu, and finally Rovaniemi deep in Lapland. He is genuinely shocked that even smaller northern Finnish cities have become so visibly Indian and immigrant-heavy. While admitting Helsinki still works, he says he would honestly rather stay put in cramped Hong Kong, where at least everyone speaks Cantonese and he does not have to wrestle with foreign bureaucracy on a…
clips.text_en_c1: A /pol/ correspondent recounts his experience arriving at Helsinki-Vantaa airport, where, to his considerable dismay, the overwhelming majority of passengers appeared to be of foreign origin. Subsequent rail travel to Tampere, Oulu, and ultimately Rovaniemi yielded an identical demographic composition, prompting him to conclude that even Finland's most northerly municipalities have undergone profound demographic transformation. He expresses a marked preference for Hong Kong's perceived homogeneity, citing the practical convenience of conducting daily affairs in Cantonese rather than navigating intercultural communication. Beneath the surface observation lies an explicitly nativist sentiment that, while crudely articulated, captures a broader anxiety regarding the pace and character of contemporary Nordic immigration policy.
clips.text_en_c2: A /pol/ correspondent recounts a journey across Finland that has evidently unsettled him in ways he did not anticipate upon booking his ticket. Upon disembarking at Helsinki-Vantaa airport, he observed an overwhelmingly non-native population; undeterred, he boarded the requisite Intercity services bound for Tampere, Oulu, and ultimately Rovaniemi, only to discover that the demographic composition remained stubbornly consistent throughout. He professes astonishment that even the comparatively diminutive municipalities of northern Finland have undergone such pronounced alteration, with Indian and other immigrant communities now conspicuously present at every station, in every queue, and apparently at every turn.

clips.text_en_b1: An eroge is currently ranked first on Steam in Japan, beating every AAA PC title on the charts. Anons in /v/ are surprised and mocking the state of Japanese PC gaming. Some point out that Japanese gamers are just tired after work and want simple comfort content.

clips.text_en_b2: An eroge has somehow climbed to number one on Steam in Japan, comfortably beating every major AAA PC release on the charts, and /v/ cannot quite get over it. While anons are busy mocking the state of Japanese PC gaming, a few are pointing out that overworked salarymen coming home wrecked simply crave low-effort comfort content rather than another punishing strategy title. The consensus is that after a long day of grind, nobody wants to think, and an eroge fits that mood perfectly.
clips.text_en_c1: An adult visual novel has unexpectedly claimed the top position on Steam's Japanese regional chart, comprehensively outselling every triple-A PC title currently available on the storefront. The development has prompted considerable incredulity among /v/ regulars, several of whom interpret the phenomenon as symptomatic of a broader decline in Japanese PC gaming standards. Others, however, advance a more sympathetic reading: given the notorious intensity of Japanese work culture, commuters and salarymen seeking evening entertainment gravitate toward low-friction, emotionally uncomplicated content requiring minimal cognitive investment. The thread thereby crystallises a familiar tension between connoisseurship and the market's actual purchasing behaviour, with comfort decisively prevailing over critical prestige.
clips.text_en_c2: The Japanese Steam storefront currently lists, at its unequivocal apex, an eroge title that has comprehensively outmanoeuvred every AAA PC release available on the platform this week, a development that /v/ anons greeted with a mixture of incredulity, derision, and grudging admiration. Several posters argued that the result, however ignominious it might appear to Western sensibilities, is entirely consonant with the lived experience of Japan's overworked salaryman class, who return home utterly spent and seek nothing more cognitively demanding than familiar, low-friction comfort content. The thread's most resonant observation, however, came from a contributor who noted, with the weary self-awareness of a man who has just endured another bruising ranked session, that he himself craves precisely the same form of disengagement after his own matches, suggesting that the cultural gulf between Tokyo and the global…

clips.text_zh: 每次cut 緊bench 都down，個個都有新excuse：cutting、shoulders 痛、屋企lift、narrow grip、lower reps⋯⋯我cut 緊都係，肥仔信話我冇excuse 要grind 😂
clips.text_en_b1: >I'm cutting, that's why my bench is going down >my shoulders are bad, that's why I don't squat anymore >I'm getting used to lifting in my living room >I started benching with a narrower grip and no leg drive >I'm sticking to lower reps to go easy on my shoulders.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread roasting classic excuses lifters use while cutting
clips.text_en_b2: A /fit/ poster is cataloguing every classic excuse lifters trot out the moment their bench stalls while cutting: blaming the cut itself, suddenly claiming bad shoulders to dodge squats, getting used to curling in the living room, switching to a narrow grip with no leg drive, or capping reps to spare the joints. He admits he is cutting too, but refuses to let himself off the hook that easily.
clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ regular compiles an exhaustive catalogue of the canonical excuses that recreational weightlifters invariably invoke whenever their bench press performance deteriorates mid-cut. Among them: the cut itself, latent shoulder pathology, improvised home-gym training, a narrower grip deliberately adopted to accommodate injury, and a reduced rep range intended to spare the joints. The poster wryly acknowledges that he, too, has recourse to such rationalisations, yet insists that the fundamental remedy remains undiminished. If one's lifts are regressing, no elaborate biomechanical explanation can substitute for disciplined effort. Anons respond with mixed amusement and grudging recognition, several confessing to deploying identical defences when confronted with stalled progression in their own training.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ poster has compiled a delightfully exhaustive catalogue of the canonical excuses that beleaguered lifters invoke whenever their bench press numbers begin to regress, and the litany is as recognisable as it is damning. It begins, inevitably, with cutting, the universal refuge of the aesthetically motivated and the perpetually recompensating, before progressing through complaints about shoulder impingement, the conveniently domestic rationale of lifting in one's living room, the technical revisionism of switching to a narrower grip whilst discreetly abandoning leg drive, and culminating in the cautious stratagem of restricting oneself to lower rep ranges to spare the joints.

clips.text_en_b1: A new /a/ viewer on Demon Slayer season 2 is asking why so many people hate on it. He thinks every criticism levelled at KnY applies equally to other beloved anime, and the only real difference is that KnY made billions at the box office. He is enjoying the show so far.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread defending Demon Slayer from haters
clips.text_en_b2: A new /a/ viewer on Demon Slayer season 2 is genuinely baffled by the amount of hate the show attracts, arguing that nearly every criticism levelled at KnY applies just as easily to dozens of beloved anime that nobody drags. He reckons the only real difference is that KnY raked in billions at the box office, making popularity itself an easy target. Having just binged a few arcs after exhausting ranked LoL sessions, he finds the animation crisp and the fights genuinely thrilling.
clips.text_en_c1: A recent initiate to Demon Slayer's second season poses a question that has long animated /a/: why does this particular series attract such disproportionate hostility from the anime community, when other equally formulaic shonen titles are received with comparative warmth? He observes that virtually every criticism levelled against Kimetsu no Yaiba, ranging from its derivative narrative scaffolding to its emotionally overwrought confrontations, applies with equal force to works held in far higher esteem. The sole distinguishing factor, he contends, is the franchise's extraordinary commercial success, which has rendered it an inviting target for those predisposed to disdain popular phenomena.
clips.text_en_c2: A newly initiated /a/ viewer of Demon Slayer's second season has posed a question that has animated fan discourse since the franchise's stratospheric commercial ascent: why, he wonders, does the anime attract such disproportionate opprobrium when the substantive criticisms levelled against it could be applied, with equal validity, to any number of beloved and critically cherished series? He observes, with the measured detachment of someone who has recently binged the entirety of the season after a punishing League of Legends session, that the only meaningful differentiator appears to be the franchise's billions at the box office, an inconvenient commercial success that has evidently transformed aesthetic reservations into something considerably more visceral.
